title: Docker Complete Handbook
summary: A start-to-production tour of Docker: architecture, images and containers, Dockerfile and build optimization, storage, networking, Compose, registries, security, debugging and orchestration, closing with a cheat sheet of commands and interview-ready practices.

chapters.title: Docker
points: Docker packages an app plus its dependencies into a portable image that runs the same on any host
Containers share the host kernel, so they start in milliseconds and use MBs, unlike VMs with a full guest OS
Handbook map: architecture, images, Dockerfile, storage, networking, Compose, registries, security, debugging, production, cheat sheet

chapters.title: Docker Architecture and Internals
points: Client-server model: the docker CLI talks over a REST API (unix socket /var/run/docker.sock) to the dockerd daemon
dockerd delegates to containerd (lifecycle, images), which calls runc (OCI runtime) to create the container process
Namespaces isolate what a process sees: pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user
cgroups limit what a process uses: CPU, memory, I/O, pids
Union filesystem (overlay2) stacks read-only image layers under one writable container layer using copy-on-write
Docker vs VM comparison: shared kernel vs hypervisor plus guest OS; seconds vs minutes boot; less isolation but far denser
Mistake: mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container gives that container root-equivalent control of the host
Interview Point: What is the difference between dockerd, containerd and runc? What do namespaces vs cgroups do? Why are containers lighter than VMs?

chapters.title: Images and Containers Lifecycle
points: Image = immutable, layered, content-addressed template; container = a running (or stopped) instance with a writable layer
Image identity: name:tag is a mutable pointer, name@sha256:digest is immutable
Lifecycle states: created, running, paused, exited, removed; commands docker create, start, stop, kill, rm
docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web nginx runs detached, publishes a port, and names the container
docker stop sends SIGTERM then SIGKILL after 10s; docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately
docker exec -it web sh opens a shell in a running container; docker run starts a new one
CMD vs ENTRYPOINT: CMD is the default command that run args override; ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable that args are appended to
Mistake: using :latest in production; it is not 'newest' and changes silently
Mistake: expecting data to survive docker rm; the writable layer is deleted with the container
Interview Point: What is the difference between an image and a container? Stop vs kill? exec vs run? CMD vs ENTRYPOINT?

chapters.title: Dockerfile Essentials
points: FROM sets the base image; every Dockerfile starts here (FROM scratch for an empty base)
RUN executes at build time and creates a layer; CMD/ENTRYPOINT define runtime behaviour
COPY vs ADD: COPY copies files only; ADD also extracts local tar and fetches URLs, so prefer COPY
WORKDIR sets the working directory and creates it; avoid RUN cd
ENV persists in the running container; ARG exists only at build time
EXPOSE only documents the port; it does not publish it
Exec form CMD ["node","app.js"] makes the app PID 1 and receives signals; shell form wraps it in /bin/sh -c
Example: FROM node:20-alpine / WORKDIR /app / COPY package*.json ./ / RUN npm ci / COPY . . / CMD ["node","server.js"]
Mistake: baking secrets into ENV or ARG; they remain visible in docker history
Interview Point: ARG vs ENV? COPY vs ADD? Exec vs shell form? Does EXPOSE publish a port?

chapters.title: Build Optimization and Multi-Stage Builds
points: Each RUN, COPY and ADD instruction creates a layer; the build cache is invalidated from the first changed instruction downward
Order from least to most frequently changing: base, dependency manifests, install, then source code
Copy package.json and install dependencies before COPY . . so code edits do not re-run the install
Chain commands in one RUN with && and clean up in the same layer (apt-get update && apt-get install -y x && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*)
A .dockerignore (node_modules, .git, .env) shrinks the build context and avoids cache busts and leaked files
Multi-stage: FROM golang AS build then FROM alpine and COPY --from=build /out/app /app ships only the artifact
Slim bases compared: ubuntu ~75MB, debian-slim ~75MB, alpine ~5MB (musl libc), distroless has no shell, scratch is empty
BuildKit adds parallel stages, cache mounts (RUN --mount=type=cache) and secret mounts (--mount=type=secret)
Mistake: deleting a file in a later layer; the earlier layer still holds it so size does not shrink
Interview Point: How does Docker layer caching work? How do you shrink an image? What is a multi-stage build and why use it? Why is instruction order important?

chapters.title: Volumes and Storage
points: Container writable layer is ephemeral and slower because of copy-on-write; persist data outside it
Named volume: managed by Docker under /var/lib/docker/volumes, created with docker volume create or -v data:/var/lib/data
Bind mount: maps a host path into the container with -v $(pwd):/app; ideal for live-reload dev, tied to host layout
tmpfs mount: held in host memory only, never written to disk; good for secrets and scratch data
Comparison: volume for production data and backups, bind mount for development, tmpfs for sensitive temporary data
--mount is explicit and verbose; -v is shorthand; a missing bind path errors with --mount but is auto-created with -v
Backup a volume by running a throwaway container that tars the mount into a bind-mounted host folder
Mistake: bind-mounting an empty host dir over a populated image path hides the image's files; an empty named volume copies them on first use
Mistake: running a database without a volume, so docker rm destroys the data
Interview Point: Volume vs bind mount vs tmpfs? Where does container data live? How do you back up a volume?

chapters.title: Docker Networking
points: Default network drivers: bridge (single host default), host, none, overlay (multi-host), macvlan (own MAC on LAN)
Default bridge docker0 gives IPs but no name resolution; a user-defined bridge adds automatic DNS by container name
Port publishing -p host:container installs iptables NAT rules; the container is unreachable from outside without it
host driver removes network isolation and port mapping, giving the best performance on Linux
Container-to-container: put both on the same user-defined network and call http://db:5432 by name
docker network create app-net then docker run --network app-net lets services find each other by name
Mistake: connecting to localhost from inside a container; localhost is the container itself, so use the service name or host.docker.internal
Mistake: binding the app to 127.0.0.1 inside the container, which makes the published port unreachable; bind 0.0.0.0
Interview Point: Bridge vs host vs overlay? Why does DNS only work on user-defined networks? How does -p work under the hood?

chapters.title: Docker Compose
points: Compose defines a multi-container app in one compose.yaml: services, networks, volumes
Commands: docker compose up -d, down (-v also removes volumes), logs -f, ps, exec, build
Example service: web with build: ., ports: ["8080:80"], depends_on: [db], environment, and db with image: postgres:16 and volumes: [pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
Compose creates a default network per project so services reach each other by service name
depends_on controls start order only; use condition: service_healthy with a healthcheck to wait for readiness
Environment: environment:, env_file:, and ${VAR} interpolation from .env
profiles enable optional services; override files (compose.override.yaml) layer dev settings on a base
Mistake: assuming depends_on waits until the database accepts connections
Mistake: running docker compose down -v and deleting database volumes unintentionally
Interview Point: Does depends_on wait for readiness? How do services discover each other? Compose vs Swarm vs Kubernetes?

chapters.title: Registries and Image Distribution
points: A registry stores and serves images: Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR, GCR/Artifact Registry, ACR, or self-hosted registry:2
Image reference format: registry/namespace/repo:tag, and a bare name defaults to docker.io/library
Workflow: docker build -t myapp:1.0 . then docker tag then docker login then docker push; pull fetches the layers you lack
Layers are content-addressed by sha256, so shared layers are stored and transferred once
Tag strategy: immutable semantic versions and git SHAs; moving tags like latest or 1.2 only for convenience
Multi-arch images use manifest lists (docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64)
Pin by digest (image@sha256:...) for reproducible deploys; set retention and lifecycle policies to prune old tags
Mistake: Docker Hub pull rate limits for anonymous users breaking CI; authenticate or mirror
Mistake: pushing images with embedded secrets to a public repository
Interview Point: What is an image digest vs tag? How do multi-arch images work? How do you make deploys reproducible?

chapters.title: Docker Security
points: Containers share the kernel, so a kernel exploit or misconfiguration can escape; isolation is weaker than a VM
Run as non-root: USER app in the Dockerfile, since root in the container is root on the host without user namespaces
Drop capabilities: --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE; avoid --privileged
Read-only root filesystem: --read-only plus tmpfs for writable paths; --security-opt no-new-privileges
Default seccomp profile blocks about 44 risky syscalls; AppArmor/SELinux add mandatory access control
Use minimal trusted base images and scan them (docker scout, Trivy) in CI; pin versions and rebuild often
Secrets: use Docker/Swarm/Kubernetes secrets or BuildKit secret mounts, never ENV, ARG or COPY
Enable Docker Content Trust or sign images with cosign to verify provenance
Mistake: exposing the Docker daemon on tcp 2375 without TLS, or mounting docker.sock
Interview Point: Why is running as root dangerous? What does --privileged do? How do you handle secrets and scan images?

chapters.title: Debugging and Troubleshooting
points: docker logs -f --tail 100 <c> shows stdout/stderr; the app must log to stdout, not to a file
docker inspect returns JSON for state, mounts, IP, env, and exit code; use --format to extract fields
docker ps -a plus exit codes: 0 clean, 1 app error, 137 SIGKILL/OOM killed, 139 segfault, 143 SIGTERM
docker stats shows live CPU, memory and network; docker top lists processes; docker events streams daemon activity
docker exec -it <c> sh to look inside; if no shell exists, use docker debug or a sidecar sharing --pid and --network
Container restarts in a loop: check logs, CMD and ENTRYPOINT, missing env vars, and port conflicts
OOMKilled shows in docker inspect State.OOMKilled; raise --memory or fix the leak
docker system df and docker system prune reclaim disk from dangling images, stopped containers and build cache
Mistake: exit code 0 immediately because the main process finished or ran in the background; a container lives as long as PID 1
Interview Point: A container exits immediately, how do you debug it? What does exit code 137 mean? How do you free disk space?

chapters.title: Production and Orchestration
points: Set --restart unless-stopped or always, and add HEALTHCHECK so the platform can detect unhealthy containers
Set resource limits (--memory, --cpus) so one container cannot starve the host
Graceful shutdown: handle SIGTERM and use exec-form CMD or --init (tini) so PID 1 forwards signals and reaps zombies
Log driver and rotation (json-file max-size, max-file) prevent logs filling the disk; ship to a central system
12-factor: config via environment, stateless containers, one process per container, logs to stdout
Single host: Compose; Docker Swarm: simple built-in clustering with docker stack deploy; Kubernetes: the industry standard orchestrator
Orchestrators add scheduling, self-healing, rolling updates, service discovery, autoscaling and secrets
Comparison: Compose is single-host, Swarm is simple multi-host, Kubernetes is powerful but complex
Mistake: running a database as a single container with no volume or backups in production
Interview Point: Why does Kubernetes replace Compose in production? How do you do zero-downtime deploys? What does a HEALTHCHECK do?

chapters.title: Docker Interview Questions and Best Practices
points: Q: Image vs container? Image is the read-only template, container is a running instance with a writable layer
Q: How does Docker isolate processes? Namespaces for visibility, cgroups for resource limits
Q: How do you reduce image size? Multi-stage builds, slim or distroless base, .dockerignore, combined RUN with cleanup
Q: How do you persist data? Named volumes or bind mounts, not the container layer
Q: How do containers talk to each other? User-defined network and service-name DNS
Best practice: pin base image versions, one concern per container, run as non-root, scan images in CI
Best practice: put rarely-changing instructions first, use .dockerignore, and prefer COPY over ADD
Best practice: log to stdout, add a HEALTHCHECK, handle SIGTERM, set resource limits
Best practice: never store secrets in images and tag releases with git SHA plus semantic version
Interview Point: Walk through what happens on docker run nginx. How would you containerize and ship a service end to end?

chapters.title: Docker Cheat Sheet
points: Build and run: docker build -t app:1.0 . | docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name app app:1.0 | docker exec -it app sh
Inspect: docker ps -a | docker logs -f app | docker inspect app | docker stats | docker top app
Cleanup: docker rm -f app | docker rmi app:1.0 | docker system prune -a | docker volume prune
Volumes and networks: docker volume create v | docker network create n | docker run -v v:/data --network n
Compose: docker compose up -d | down | logs -f | ps | exec svc sh | build
Registry: docker login | docker tag app:1.0 repo/app:1.0 | docker push | docker pull
Dockerfile keywords: FROM RUN COPY WORKDIR ENV ARG EXPOSE USER HEALTHCHECK ENTRYPOINT CMD
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error, 137 killed or OOM, 139 segfault, 143 SIGTERM
Interview Point: Which five Docker commands do you use daily? How do you clean disk space safely?
